body:
Partners Group is pressing ahead with a broad overhaul of its fund lineup while management puts its own money behind the stock. The Swiss asset manager's shares have been under sustained pressure, closing yesterday at EUR 639.20, down 1.3%, extending a year-to-date decline that has now reached 40%. A separate reading earlier put the price at EUR 641.40.

At the center of the restructuring is the Global Value SICAV, the firm's private equity evergreen vehicle, which carried a net asset value of EUR 6.6 billion. After a wave of redemption requests overwhelmed previously capped payouts, Partners Group unveiled plans in early October to divide the fund into two sleeves — one targeting long-term value growth, the other distributing accumulated returns to investors. The split is designed to give institutional clients better control over their liquidity needs.

London-listed trust opts for wind-down

A parallel decision landed at Partners Group Private Equity Limited, the UK-listed investment company. Reuters reported that 74.1% of shareholders backed the liquidity option, choosing an orderly wind-down of the entire portfolio over a proposed restructuring. Votes in favor of the liquidation ultimately totaled 99.89%. Distributions to investors are scheduled to begin on March 31, 2027, paid out in half-yearly tranches. The vote applies solely to this managed entity and not to Partners Group Holding AG itself.

Alongside the wind-down, the board approved additional capital for share support measures. A residual amount of roughly EUR 4.8 million will be supplemented by a fresh EUR 10 million authorization for buybacks, valid through January 31, 2027. For the quarter ending September 30, 2026, the vehicle also reported portfolio distributions of EUR 4.8 million.

Private credit push gathers pace

Partners Group is simultaneously expanding its credit business on a selective basis. On Monday, the firm acted as senior lender on behalf of its clients in the refinancing of DELABO.group. The financing package comprises unitranche and super-senior facilities as well as additional lines for acquisitions, investments and working capital.

On the product side, the company launched a global, multi-sector private credit income strategy housed in an open-ended evergreen vehicle. Aimed at both institutional and private investors, the offering targets high single-digit to low double-digit returns, generated predominantly from recurring income.

Insiders step in, but headwinds persist

Management has been signaling confidence through personal purchases. Between October 6 and 8, executives acquired roughly CHF 21 million worth of shares on their own account, according to media reports. Since the start of September, purchases by the board and management have totaled nearly CHF 39 million. Such moves underscore internal conviction, though they have yet to reverse the broader market reticence.

That caution has been reinforced by macro forces. Hotter US inflation data rekindled rate worries across international trading venues, a dynamic that weighs doubly on private markets managers. A persistently elevated rate environment complicates dealmaking, compresses valuation multiples on unlisted holdings and keeps institutional clients on the sidelines when it comes to new commitments.

For now, the market's focus rests on whether the combination of portfolio reshaping, capital discipline and credit expansion can stabilize liquidity flows across the existing vehicles — the decisive factor for any lasting recovery in the share price.
